title: Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States
articleTitle: Judicial Standards and the Evolution of Federal Research Incentives: A Comprehensive Analysis of Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States and the Shifting Landscape of Qualified Research Expenditures
court: United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas
subject: Business Component Test
summary: Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States (N.D. Tex. 2010; 5th Cir. 2014) is a key federal R&D tax credit case under I.R.C. § 41 for U.S. taxpayers claiming first-in-class products as pilot models. Courts allowed custom vessels as prototypes but disallowed whole-vessel claims failing the 80% process-of-experimentation test because Trinity lacked subcomponent cost records needed for shrink-back.

body.text: Executive Summary & Case Background
Factual and Procedural Posture

The federal tax refund litigation in Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 691 F. Supp. 2d 688 (N.D. Tex. 2010) (Trinity I), aff'd in part, vacated in part, and remanded, 757 F.3d 400 (5th Cir. 2014) (Trinity II), stands as a foundational precedent in United States jurisprudence governing the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41). During its fiscal years ending March 31, 1994, and March 31, 1995 (the claim years), Trinity Industries, Inc. and its shipbuilding subsidiaries designed and constructed custom, first-in-class marine vessels for commercial and government customers. On its amended federal income tax returns for 1994 and 1995, Trinity claimed research tax credits under I.R.C. § 41 on the theory that its expenditures incurred in engineering, fabricating, and testing these first-in-class vessels constituted qualified research expenses (QREs). Notably, although Trinity's amended tax returns reported fixed base percentages of 1.3152% for the taxable year ending March 1994 and 1.3125% for the taxable year ending March 1995, the returns themselves did not report the base period QREs or the base period gross receipts used to calculate those fixed base percentages.

In 2001, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) issued a formal claim disallowance letter denying the refund claims in their entirety. Trinity subsequently initiated a federal tax refund suit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas, ultimately asserting entitlement to research tax credits totaling $1,808,832.53 for fiscal year 1994 and $2,712,977.00 for fiscal year 1995. The district court conducted the proceedings as a two-phase bench trial, considering six claim-year vessel projects in Phase I and two further vessel projects, together with the method of calculating Trinity's base period QREs, in Phase II.

In Phase I (Trinity I), the district court evaluated six vessel development projects from the claim years: the Mark V Special Operations Craft, the Dirty Oil Barge, the XFPB (Extra Fast Patrol Boat), the T-AGS 60 oceanographic survey ship, the Crew Rescue Boat, and the Hurley Dredge. In Phase II, the district court evaluated two additional claim-year vessel projects—the Queen of New Orleans riverboat casino and the Penn Tugs (two articulated tug-barge vessels)—alongside the methodology for computing Trinity's base period QREs under the statutory consistency rule of I.R.C. § 41(c)(6)(A). After Phase II and additional briefing, the district court entered a final judgment awarding Trinity a research tax credit of only $135,787.60 for 1994 and $0 for 1995. Trinity appealed the judgment to the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The IRS denied Trinity's refund claims in their entirety, and the ensuing administrative and federal litigation turned on four interconnected legal and evidentiary fronts. First, the litigation addressed whether custom, commercial shipbuilding contracts—where the resulting hull is delivered and sold to a customer in the ordinary course of business—could be treated in their entirety as experimental "pilot models" or prototypes whose direct material and production labor costs qualify as QREs under I.R.C. §§ 41 and 174. Second, even where vessel design involved localized pockets of engineering uncertainty, the question was whether routine hull fabrication, standard marine outfitting, systems integration, and adaptations of pre-existing or third-party vessel designs predominated. Consequently, each project had to satisfy the mandate under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) that "substantially all" (at least 80%) of the research activities measured on a cost basis constitute elements of a process of experimentation.

Third, because Trinity took an "all or nothing" approach, claiming the costs of developing entire vessels without offering proof of its expenses at the subcomponent level (partly because Hurricane Katrina destroyed many of its records), the district court could not apply the "shrinking-back rule" of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to award partial credits for experimental subsystems on vessels that failed the 80% test at the whole-vessel level. Fourth, regarding the Penn Tugs, Trinity argued that a conclusion in an IRS Revenue Agent Report (RAR), incorporated into the claim disallowance letter, finding the process-of-experimentation element satisfied either bound the United States or was entitled to a presumption of correctness; both the district court and the Fifth Circuit held that it was neither binding nor presumptively correct in a de novo refund trial. Relatedly, regarding the credit calculation formula, the district court rejected Trinity's first consistency-rule argument in Phase II and did not address its second argument, which sought to remove four allegedly non-experimental vessels from its base period QREs for the taxable years ending March 31, 1985 through March 31, 1989.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

Under United States federal tax law, tax credits are a matter of legislative grace, and the taxpayer bears the burden of proving entitlement to the claimed credit by a preponderance of the evidence. The statutory architecture governing Trinity's claim under I.R.C. § 41 comprises two interdependent regimes: the qualitative and quantitative qualification of research expenditures under I.R.C. § 41(b) and (d), and the incremental base-period computation mechanics under I.R.C. § 41(a) and (c).

To qualify as a QRE under I.R.C. § 41(b)(1), an expenditure must represent either an "in-house research expense" (wages paid to employees engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research, plus supplies used in the conduct of qualified research under § 41(b)(2)) or a "contract research expense" (65% of amounts paid to non-employees for qualified research under § 41(b)(3)). Under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1), underlying activities constitute "qualified research" only if they satisfy a conjunctive Four-Part Test applied separately to each "business component," which is defined in § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business.

The first prong of the Four-Part Test, the Section 174 Test under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), requires that expenditures be eligible to be treated as expenses under I.R.C. § 174, meaning they are incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), a "pilot model" is defined as any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement, including a fully-functional representation or model of the product. The second prong, the Technological Information Test under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), mandates that the research be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, meaning the process of experimentation fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science as specified in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4).

The third prong, the Business Component and Permitted Purpose Test under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3)(A), requires that the taxpayer intend the discovered information to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer for a qualified purpose—specifically, a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality, rather than style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors excluded under § 41(d)(3)(B). The fourth prong, the Process of Experimentation and "Substantially All" Test under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), dictates that substantially all of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a qualified purpose. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5), a process of experimentation is a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" requirement is satisfied only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities for each business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose.

When an overall business component, such as an entire marine vessel, fails the Four-Part Test—most commonly because less than 80% of its total research and development costs involve a process of experimentation—Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) mandates the application of the shrinking-back rule. Under this regulatory mechanism, the Four-Part Test is reapplied to the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention, such as an integrated propulsion system or hull sonar array. This shrinking-back continues recursively until either a subset of elements of the product that satisfies the requirements is reached, or the most basic element of the product is reached and fails to satisfy the test.

Once claim-year QREs (QRECY) are established, the regular research credit under I.R.C. § 41(a)(1) and § 41(c) equals 20% of the excess of QRECY over the "base amount" (BA), subject to the statutory minimum base amount floor under I.R.C. § 41(c)(2) whereby BA cannot be less than 50% of QRECY. Mathematically, the credit is expressed as:
Credit = 20% × [QRECY − max(BA, 50% × QRECY)]
where the base amount BA is computed under I.R.C. § 41(c)(1) and (3) as:
BA = Fixed-Base Percentage × average annual gross receipts for the four taxable years preceding the credit year

and the Fixed-Base Percentage for an established taxpayer is the ratio (capped at 16%) of aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts during the statutory base period, defined as taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989, which for Trinity's fiscal years comprised the taxable years ending March 31, 1985 through March 31, 1989. Crucially, I.R.C. § 41(c)(6)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(d)(1) establish the Consistency Rule, which mandates that the QREs taken into account in computing the fixed-base percentage must be determined on a basis consistent with the determination of QREs for the credit year.
The Courts' Final Holdings

Across the two-phase bench trial and appellate review, the federal courts issued a nuanced set of rulings that granted Trinity a vital legal victory on the treatment of first-in-class custom ships as prototypes and the enforcement of the base-period consistency rule, while penalizing the company severely for its lack of subcomponent cost accounting. In the Phase I rulings (Trinity I, 691 F. Supp. 2d 688), the district court rejected the government's categorical position that custom commercial vessels built for sale cannot constitute experimental prototypes, holding that first-in-class ships can qualify as business components and pilot models whose direct construction and material costs are includible in QREs because the ship could not be developed without them. Applying an "all-or-nothing" whole-vessel analysis necessitated by Trinity's lack of subcomponent cost records, the district court held that two of the six Phase I vessels—the Mark V and the Dirty Oil Barge—satisfied all four requirements of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1), including the 80% process-of-experimentation threshold. Conversely, the district court disallowed 100% of the claimed expenses for the remaining four vessels—the XFPB, T-AGS 60, Crew Rescue Boat, and Hurley Dredge—because their whole-vessel development costs fell below the 80% experimentation threshold and the evidentiary record contained no subcomponent cost breakdown to permit application of the shrinking-back rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2).

In the Phase II district court rulings, the court held that Trinity was entitled to QREs for the Queen of New Orleans casino vessel, but denied all credits for the first and second Penn Tugs because they failed the 80% process-of-experimentation requirement. After additional briefing, the district court entered final judgment for only $135,787.60 for 1994 and $0 for 1995, figures identical to those in Trinity's post-trial briefing, which used the base amounts derived from the base period QREs and fixed base percentage in Trinity's expert (Bennett) report.

On appeal in Trinity II, 757 F.3d 400, the Fifth Circuit affirmed in part, and vacated and remanded in part. First, the Fifth Circuit rejected Trinity's contention that the district court violated the consistency rule by applying a shrink-back methodology in the base period while applying an all-or-nothing methodology in the claim years, finding that the district court actually utilized an all-or-nothing expert calculation across both periods. Second, the Fifth Circuit agreed with Trinity that I.R.C. § 41(c)(6)(A) requires symmetric application of the Phase I QRE qualification standard to base-period projects. Because Trinity presented testimony from its former Vice President of Engineering (Phil Nuss) that four base-period vessels (LSV, North Carolina Auto Ferry, Cajun Queen, and Ecuador) were no more experimental than the four disqualified Phase I vessels, supported by testimony from its former Chief Project Engineer (Sam Charters) that the LSV was comparable to the Hurley Dredge, and the district court failed to make factual findings on whether to credit that testimony, the Fifth Circuit vacated the district court's consistency-rule holding and remanded for a limited factual finding: if the district court credits the testimony, those four vessels must be removed from the base period, reducing base period QREs to $26,706,987, which would lower Trinity's fixed base percentage and increase its claim-year tax credits, whereas any of the four vessels found more experimental than the disqualified claim-year vessels and sufficiently experimental to qualify must remain in the base period. Third, the Fifth Circuit affirmed the complete disallowance of QREs for the Penn Tugs, holding that a subsidiary finding in an IRS Revenue Agent Report is neither binding on the government nor entitled to a presumption of correctness in a de novo refund suit, that the district court did not err in analyzing the first and second Penn Tugs separately and sequentially because Trinity cited no authority requiring them to be treated together and did not show that combining them would surpass the 80% threshold, and that Trinity failed to prove that 80% of the Penn Tugs' development activities constituted a scientific process of experimentation.

body.text: Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures
The All-or-Nothing Litigation Trap and Failure to Trigger the Shrinking-Back Rule

The single most destructive evidentiary failure in Trinity Industries was the taxpayer's inability to segregate and substantiate costs at the subcomponent or subsystem level, forcing it into an "all-or-nothing" litigation posture. When a taxpayer defines its "business component" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B) as an entire custom-built capital asset—such as a 329-foot oceanographic survey ship (T-AGS 60) or a specialized patrol vessel (XFPB)—the denominator of the "substantially all" fraction under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) expands to encompass all research and development activities (and, for pilot models, associated direct production activities deductible under § 174) undertaken on that entire vessel.

To capture 100% of the vessel construction costs as QREs, at least 80% of the total activities and costs in that denominator must constitute elements of a process of experimentation in the numerator. In large-scale manufacturing and shipbuilding, even highly complex vessels involve massive expenditures for standard structural steel fabrication, routine piping and electrical runs, commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) equipment installation, and conventional marine architecture. Consequently, when the district court determined that less than 80% of the total costs of the XFPB, T-AGS 60, Crew Rescue Boat, Hurley Dredge, and Penn Tugs involved a process of experimentation, the whole-vessel business components failed I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C).

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), the failure of the whole vessel should immediately trigger the shrinking-back rule, allowing the taxpayer to step down to discrete experimental subcomponents—for example, the acoustic sonar hull-mount integration on the T-AGS 60, the high-speed propulsion hydrodynamics on the XFPB, or the structural wave-action interface supporting the articulating coupler on the Penn Tugs. However, the shrinking-back rule is not a judicial estimation device; it requires independent quantitative proof of the costs incurred on each specific subset of elements. Because Trinity did not offer proof of its claim-year expenses at the subcomponent level—an inability attributable in part to Hurricane Katrina's destruction of many of its records—the court had no evidence of the labor and supply costs attributable to specific vessel subcomponents. As the district court expressly noted in its Phase II order when rejecting Trinity's first consistency-rule argument, the court applied the 80% rule only to entire projects "due to a lack of evidence to permit application of the shrinkback rule," which "simply reflects the absence of evidence of costs incurred on a subset of an entire vessel"; the Fifth Circuit quoted this passage but did not adopt it as its own holding, observing instead that the district court had failed to acknowledge that Trinity's base period QREs were themselves computed on an all-or-nothing basis, and it ultimately vacated the district court's consistency-rule holding.

Furthermore, while Trinity I permitted the Mark V and Dirty Oil Barge to pass the 80% whole-vessel threshold based largely on their overarching novelty—with the trial court remarking that it did "not intend to enumerate everything about the [ship] that was new and required research expenditures"—subsequent United States appellate precedent has closed that leniency. In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), aff'g T.C. Memo. 2021-15, the Seventh Circuit and the U.S. Tax Court explicitly rejected Trinity I's "heuristic of newness" or "feels new enough" approach. Modern U.S. courts strictly require taxpayers to establish both the numerator (activities constituting elements of a process of experimentation, including pilot model production activities only to the extent the model is used to evaluate alternatives through a scientific process of experimentation) and the denominator of the 80% fraction via rigorous quantitative accounting rather than relying on the general novelty of a first-in-class vessel.
Deficiencies in Proving a Structured Process of Experimentation and Technological Uncertainty

A second core failure in Trinity Industries was the conflation of standard engineering design, regulatory reconfiguration, and routine manufacturing adjustments with a true scientific "process of experimentation" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5). Relying on established federal precedent—including United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009), Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), and United States v. Davenport, 897 F. Supp. 2d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2012)—the Fifth Circuit emphasized that a process of experimentation requires the identification of uncertainty, the identification of one or more alternatives intended to eliminate it, and a process of evaluating those alternatives, which at a minimum must involve a systematic trial and error methodology: a methodical plan involving a series of trials to test a hypothesis, analyze the data, refine the hypothesis, and retest the hypothesis, as opposed to simple trial and error used to validate that a change meets the taxpayer's needs.

This evidentiary deficiency manifested acutely across multiple disqualified vessels. In developing the first Penn Tug, Trinity conducted some computer modeling, testing, retesting, and four design revisions to modify an existing hull design and evaluate the structural integrity of the tug-coupler combination under wave action. However, although the Fifth Circuit accepted that designing the hull involved some systematic experimentation, it held that Trinity failed to establish which other aspects of its research involved systematic trial and error, and it found no error in the district court's finding that the hull design was based to some extent on an existing design, involved modifications of old hulls, and retained similarities to existing hulls, so that those hull revisions did not transform the entire tug construction project into an 80% experimental endeavor.

A similar failure occurred regarding regulatory material substitution and sequential prototype splitting between the first and second Penn Tugs. Between the construction of the two vessels, changes in U.S. Coast Guard fire regulations compelled Trinity to change the material composition of the elevated pilot house from aluminum (used on the first tug to minimize topside weight and maintain stability) to heavier steel on the second tug. While the heavier steel pilot house required other design changes, the district court found that the only process of experimentation between the first and second tugs was the change in pilot-house composition, and the Fifth Circuit noted that although Trinity said it "experimented" with an aluminum tower and pilothouse, it did not allege that designing the tower involved the kind of systematic trial and error that the hull design involved. Moreover, Trinity argued on appeal that the district court erred by evaluating the first and second Penn Tugs separately and sequentially rather than aggregating them as a single development project. The Fifth Circuit rejected this argument, holding that it was not error to consider the two tugs separately and sequentially because Trinity cited no authority requiring the court to treat them together and, even if it had, failed to show how combining them would push the aggregate experimental activities over the 80% threshold.

Furthermore, Trinity's overarching commercial goal in designing the Penn Tugs as an articulated tug barge (ATB) was regulatory arbitrage: a large integrated cargo ship required a 20-person crew with advanced Coast Guard licenses, whereas a separately certified tug and barge connected by a coupler could be operated by a much smaller crew with simpler licenses. The Fifth Circuit recited this crew-licensing objective as background but did not treat it as evidence of a process of experimentation; its analysis turned instead on whether Trinity proved systematic trial and error across substantially all of its research activities on the tugs themselves. Likewise, the Phase I Crew Rescue Boat, Hurley Dredge, and XFPB projects failed the 80% test; according to the Phase II testimony, the Hurley Dredge was built from a design provided by a third party, the Crew Rescue Boat was not a technologically complicated vessel to build, and the XFPB had some experimental features but not enough to qualify, while the district court found that the integration of subsystems on these projects did not rise to the level required for the cost of the entire vessel to qualify.
Third-Party Engineering, Customer-Supplied Designs, and Unallocated Integration Costs

Trinity Industries also exposes the fatal flaw of claiming whole-product QREs when the core technological innovation or baseline design originates with a third party rather than the taxpayer. Under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), qualified research must be undertaken to discover technological information useful in the development of a business component of the taxpayer.

In the Penn Tugs project, the technological linchpin of the articulated tug-barge concept was the articulating mechanical arm—the "Intercon coupler"—that locked the tug into the barge notch so the tug could function as the barge's propeller in open seas. However, the evidence at trial revealed that the Intercon coupler system was invented, developed, and manufactured entirely by third-party companies. Trinity did not invent, design, or fabricate the coupler; it merely worked alongside the third-party manufacturer to design the structural support housing within the tug hull to receive the coupler. Both the district court and the Fifth Circuit held that the court properly excluded the coupler itself from Trinity's research evaluation and focused strictly on Trinity's internal activities on the tugs. Because Trinity lacked subcomponent cost tracking to isolate the hours spent by its structural engineers modeling the wave-load forces on the coupler support structure (a potential shrink-back subset), the exclusion of the third-party coupler left Trinity's claim dependent on its research activities on the tugs themselves, where it showed some systematic experimentation in the hull design but failed to establish that substantially all of its research activities involved such experimentation.

Similarly, on the claim-year Hurley Dredge (as well as the base-period LSV and North Carolina Auto Ferry), Trinity constructed the vessels based on designs provided to Trinity by third parties, with Charters testifying that the LSV was based in part on an existing design. When a manufacturer constructs a custom product from customer-supplied drawings, the baseline design uncertainty has already been resolved by an external party; unless the manufacturer isolates its internal production-process improvements or specific subsystem redesigns via the shrinking-back rule, the overall build will fail the Four-Part Test.
Misplaced Evidentiary Reliance on IRS Revenue Agent Reports and Burden of Proof Failures

A critical procedural failure occurred during Phase II regarding the Penn Tugs, where Trinity attempted to substitute an audit-stage administrative finding for affirmative trial proof. Specifically, when the IRS issued its 2001 claim disallowance letter, it incorporated an underlying Revenue Agent Report (RAR) in which the examining agent had concluded that the fourth QRE requirement (process of experimentation) was satisfied for the Penn Tugs, even though two other QRE requirements were not. At trial and on appeal, Trinity argued that because the disallowance letter incorporated the RAR, the United States was either conclusively bound by the agent's subsidiary conclusion or, at a minimum, a legal "presumption of correctness" attached to the RAR finding that shifted the burden to the government to rebut it with affirmative evidence.

The Fifth Circuit flatly rejected this argument, applying a vital litigation principle for federal tax refund suits. In a tax refund action brought in federal district court, the court reviews de novo the Commissioner's ultimate determination of the taxpayer's tax liability. While the Commissioner's ultimate tax assessment—the final determination of tax liability—is cloaked in a presumption of correctness that requires the taxpayer to bear both the burden of production (going forward with evidence) and the burden of persuasion by a preponderance of the evidence, that presumption does not attach to the subsidiary factual conclusions or legal rationales stated by an IRS revenue agent in an administrative report. Under the Federal Rules of Evidence, an RAR is admissible evidence, but it is neither conclusive nor binding on the Department of Justice or the trial court. Because the RAR's conclusion carried no binding force or presumption, Trinity had to carry its burden on the merits, and the testimony it offered (showing some systematic experimentation in the hull design but not in its other research activities) did not prove that 80% of the Penn Tugs' research activities constituted elements of a process of experimentation, so Trinity failed to carry its burden of persuasion.
Base Period Consistency Omissions and Amended Return Deficiencies

Finally, Trinity's tax reporting and litigation posture suffered from severe base-period accounting deficiencies that nearly wiped out the value of the credits it won on the Mark V, Dirty Oil Barge, and Queen of New Orleans. When Trinity originally filed its amended returns for 1994 and 1995, it reported only its fixed base percentages and did not report the base period QREs or base period gross receipts for the taxable years ending March 31, 1985 through March 31, 1989 used to compute them. In computing its fixed-base percentage on the amended returns, Trinity included ten base-period vessel projects in its base period QRE pool (calculated by its expert at $49,483,136, based on 100% of the wages, supplies, and contract labor costs for those vessels, less overhead), selecting only those vessels it believed were sufficiently experimental for the entire vessel to constitute qualified research under its pre-litigation view of what constituted a qualified prototype vessel.

However, once the district court issued its Phase I order disqualifying four of the six claim-year vessels (XFPB, T-AGS 60, Crew Rescue Boat, and Hurley Dredge) under a much stricter application of the 80% process-of-experimentation standard, an acute mathematical asymmetry arose. Leaving all ten vessels inside the base period inflated the fixed-base percentage and the base amount (BA), thereby swallowing up the reduced claim-year QREs (QRECY) and yielding $0 in credit for 1995 and only $135,787.60 for 1994.

In Phase II, Trinity presented testimony from former Vice President of Engineering Phil Nuss that, under the standard articulated in Trinity I, four of the ten base-period vessels—the LSV and North Carolina Auto Ferry (built from third-party designs like the disallowed Hurley Dredge), the Cajun Queen (technologically simple like the disallowed Crew Rescue Boat), and the Ecuador (containing insufficient experimental features like the disallowed XFPB)—would no longer qualify as QREs, together with testimony from former Chief Project Engineer Sam Charters that the LSV was comparable to the Hurley Dredge. Although Trinity's first consistency-rule argument, that the district court inconsistently applied the shrink-back rule to the base period, failed (because both periods were evaluated on an all-or-nothing basis), the Fifth Circuit held that the district court erred by failing to address whether those four base-period vessels should be excluded under I.R.C. § 41(c)(6)(A), and it vacated and remanded for a factual finding on whether to credit the Nuss and Charters testimony. This aspect of the ruling underscores that taxpayers must proactively audit and align their historical base-period project pool with the exact legal and evidentiary filters applied to their credit-year projects.

Relied on a favorable POE statement in an IRS RAR incorporated into the claim disallowance letter for the Penn Tugs, arguing it bound the government or created a presumption of correctness.

Refund suits are reviewed de novo; the taxpayer bears both the burden of production and persuasion by a preponderance of the evidence. Subsidiary RAR findings are admissible evidence but carry no presumption of correctness and do not bind the government.

Reported only fixed base percentages, without the underlying base period QREs or gross receipts, on amended returns; included ten vessels in the base period (taxable years ending March 31, 1985 through March 31, 1989), four of which (LSV, N.C. Auto Ferry, Cajun Queen, Ecuador) Trinity's witnesses testified would not satisfy the stricter Trinity I standard.

QREs included in the fixed-base percentage must be determined using the same QRE definition and the same standard for whether a project is sufficiently experimental as applied to credit-year QREs, including the same types of expenditures; the Fifth Circuit did not decide whether the shrinking-back rule itself must be applied consistently across both periods, because the lack of base period records apparently precluded its application there.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies
Case Study 1: Custom Maritime & Autonomous Offshore Vessel Manufacturer

In this first applied scenario, a United States Gulf Coast commercial shipyard ("GulfStream Marine Corp.") is contracted to design and construct a first-in-class 290-foot Autonomous Offshore Wind Service Vessel (AOWSV-1) with a total build cost of $42,000,000. The vessel incorporates a motion-compensated gangway and an active heave-compensated crane invented and manufactured by a third-party European supplier, alongside a novel hybrid-methanol electric propulsion plant and an acoustic dynamic-positioning (DP-3) hull form engineered internally by GulfStream.

If GulfStream follows Trinity's historical practices, it will encounter four fatal Trinity Industries pitfalls. First, claiming the entire $42,000,000 vessel as a single "all-or-nothing" pilot model business component will fail the 80% "substantially all" test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) because standard steel hull fabrication, crew quarters outfitting, and commercial-off-the-shelf piping constitute 62% of total vessel costs. Second, failing to maintain subcomponent cost accounting will foreclose the shrinking-back rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). Third, including the third-party motion-compensated gangway and crane in its QRE base will mirror the disallowed Intercon coupler in the Penn Tugs. Fourth, storing physical shipyard job tickets locally exposes the company to catastrophic evidentiary loss from Gulf Coast hurricanes without cloud-replicated subcomponent ledgers.
Step 1: Project Governance and Business Component Hierarchy

Before cutting steel or logging engineering hours, GulfStream's tax and naval engineering leadership must replace macro hull-level job costing with a three-tier Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) mapped directly to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). Under this governance structure, Tier 1 represents the macro business component, designated as Hull #401 (AOWSV-1 Complete Vessel). Tier 2 divides the vessel into major functional subsystems that serve as the primary shrink-back level: WBS 401.10 captures the standard hull structure, superstructure, and crew accommodations, which are classified upfront as non-qualified routine production; WBS 401.20 isolates the hybrid-methanol propulsion and cryogenic fuel containment system as Qualified Shrink-Back Component A; WBS 401.30 isolates the acoustic DP-3 thruster hull-integration and anti-cavitation skeg geometry as Qualified Shrink-Back Component B; and WBS 401.40 isolates the structural wave-load foundation and active control interface for the third-party gangway as Qualified Shrink-Back Component C.

Within each Tier 2 subsystem, Tier 3 establishes discrete sub-assemblies and activity codes that serve as a secondary shrink-back level, utilizing sub-accounts that segregate conceptual CAD and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling (.01), prototype component fabrication (.02), dockside and sea-trial hypothesis testing (.03), and routine quality-control inspection (.04). All WBS ledgers, engineering drawings, and employee timesheets must be replicated daily to an immutable, geographically distributed cloud Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) environment, eliminating the single-point-of-failure catastrophe caused by Hurricane Katrina in Trinity Industries.
Step 2: Technical Documentation of Uncertainty and Process of Experimentation

To survive judicial scrutiny under both Trinity II and Little Sandy Coal, GulfStream must prohibit reliance on the "newness" or "first-in-class" label of AOWSV-1 and instead mandate contemporaneous Technical Uncertainty and Experimentation Dossiers for each Tier 2 WBS component. Prior to concept design, the Chief Naval Architect must author an Objective Uncertainty Charter documenting why publicly available marine engineering standards (such as American Bureau of Shipping and U.S. Coast Guard rules) cannot establish the appropriate design or method for isolating vibrations from the third-party gangway foundation (WBS 401.40) without inducing harmonic resonance in the acoustic DP-3 sensors (WBS 401.30).

Throughout development, marine engineers must log every CFD run, finite element analysis (FEA) stress iteration, and towing-tank scale model test in a structured narrative and empirical matrix that records the specific hypothesis formulated (for example, that an asymmetric twin-skeg geometry at a 14-degree deadrise will reduce thruster cavitation noise below 110 decibels), the simulation or trial executed, the empirical data output, the resulting design refinements across revisions one through five, and the final retest validation. Crucially, for WBS 401.40, technical documentation must explicitly exclude the purchase price and third-party vendor engineering of the European gangway—mirroring the exclusion of the Intercon coupler in the Penn Tugs—while rigorously documenting GulfStream's internal FEA modeling and structural weld-configuration trials required to integrate the gangway's dynamic load profile into the vessel's main deck framing.
Step 3: Contract Terms and Risk Allocation

When custom vessels are built under commercial or government contracts, the IRS frequently challenges whether the research is "funded" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), or whether the vessel is built from a design provided by a third party, as with the disallowed Hurley Dredge. GulfStream's legal counsel must structure the shipbuilding contract with four protective provisions. First, the contract must be drafted as a firm fixed-price agreement tied to strict functional performance guarantees—such as bollard pull, methanol fuel consumption rate, station-keeping tolerance in Sea State 6, and acoustic signature thresholds—rather than a build-to-print contract based on customer-supplied drawings, thereby avoiding the Hurley Dredge and LSV disqualification.

Second, a conditional acceptance and financial risk clause must explicitly stipulate that milestone progress payments are financing advances subject to full refund or builder-funded remediation until AOWSV-1 successfully passes open-water sea trials validating all performance specifications, ensuring that payment is contingent on the success of the research under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). Third, a substantial rights retention clause must reserve to GulfStream a perpetual, royalty-free ownership right or non-exclusive commercial license to use all naval architectural innovations, hull lines, methanol fuel-piping schematics, and structural integration designs developed during the build on future vessels for any customer, satisfying the "substantial rights" requirement of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(3) and the business component test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B). Fourth, in subcontracts with the European gangway supplier, the contract must demarcate the vendor's commercial-off-the-shelf equipment price from GulfStream's internal structural integration engineering so the IRS cannot conflate third-party procurement with GulfStream's internal QREs.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Base Period Consistency

To establish an unassailable quantitative nexus, GulfStream must require all naval architects, marine engineers, draftsmen, and direct fabrication supervisors to record time contemporaneously on a bi-weekly phase-gate basis in the ERP system by Tier 2 and Tier 3 WBS codes, accompanied by mandatory activity descriptors distinguishing experimental prototype fabrication and testing from routine production assembly. Rather than dumping $42,000,000 of whole-ship materials and shipyard labor into the QRE pool, GulfStream applies the shrinking-back rule upfront to WBS 401.20, 401.30, and 401.40. Within those three qualified subsystems, GulfStream includes in the numerator of the 80% fraction only the engineering wages and direct prototype fabrication labor incurred to resolve the documented technical uncertainties, ensuring each subsystem achieves an experimentation ratio exceeding 85% to 92%.

Finally, whether computing the credit under the Regular Credit of I.R.C. § 41(a)(1) or the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) of I.R.C. § 41(c)(4), GulfStream must conduct a formal Base Period Consistency Audit under I.R.C. § 41(c)(5)(A) (the current designation of the former § 41(c)(6)(A) applied in Trinity) and, for the ASC, the parallel consistency requirement for prior-year QREs in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9, by applying the exact same Tier 2 shrink-back filter to its base-period vessels. Any base-period vessel costs that represented whole-hull routine fabrication or third-party build-to-print vessels—analogous to the LSV, North Carolina Auto Ferry, Cajun Queen, and Ecuador—must be systematically removed from the base period QRE pool before filing the return, accompanied by a Contemporaneous Consistency Disclosure Statement.
Case Study 2: Heavy Industrial & Aerospace Propulsion Systems Integrator

In this second applied scenario, a United States manufacturer of heavy industrial gas-turbine gensets and auxiliary aerospace power units ("AeroTherm Dynamics, Inc.") develops two sequential generations of a high-efficiency hydrogen-blend turbine enclosure: Prototype Unit 1 (HT-100A, built with a titanium-alloy acoustic containment shroud) and Prototype Unit 2 (HT-100B, built six months later where updated Federal Aviation Administration [FAA] and occupational fire-safety standards force a switch from titanium to a heavy nickel-superalloy containment shroud, necessitating rotor-bearing load adjustments and cooling-duct rerouting). During an initial IRS examination of an amended return, an IRS engineer informally indicates in a draft Engineering and Valuation Report that the HT-100B satisfies the process-of-experimentation test, but the IRS Appeals Office subsequently issues a formal notice of disallowance.

AeroTherm faces the exact legal traps that defeated Trinity on the Penn Tugs in Phase II and at the Fifth Circuit. First, attempting to lump HT-100A and HT-100B together as a single combined business component to dilute the non-experimental manufacturing costs of HT-100B is unlikely to succeed, because in Trinity II the Fifth Circuit found no error in analyzing sequential units separately where the taxpayer cited no authority requiring joint treatment and could not show that aggregation would surpass the 80% threshold. Second, assuming that a material substitution mandated by updated safety or fire regulations (switching from titanium to nickel-superalloy, identical to the aluminum-to-steel pilot house switch on the second Penn Tug) automatically renders the entire second unit an experimental prototype will fail the process-of-experimentation test. Third, claiming routine tooling adjustments and legacy turbine frame modifications as qualified research will dilute the 80% fraction. Fourth, relying in litigation on the IRS engineer's favorable draft report rather than building an independent, de novo evidentiary record will result in a complete failure of proof.
Step 1: Project Governance and Sequential Prototype Segregation

To prevent the sequential disqualification that befell the first and second Penn Tugs, AeroTherm must establish a Sequential Prototype and Engineering Change Order (ECO) Governance Protocol. Under this protocol, AeroTherm treats HT-100A and HT-100B from inception as distinct business components in its project accounting system. Because HT-100B reuses 70% of the core turbine compressor, fuel injectors, and electronic control architecture already proven on HT-100A, HT-100B as a whole unit will inevitably fail the 80% "substantially all" threshold under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6).

Therefore, AeroTherm must configure HT-100B in its accounting ledger not as a whole-unit prototype, but as two discrete Shrink-Back Sub-Components under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2): Component HT-100B-Sub1 (the Nickel-Superalloy Thermal and Acoustic Shroud Assembly) and Component HT-100B-Sub2 (the High-Load Hydrostatic Rotor-Bearing Damping System, which had to be redesigned to support the 40% heavier superalloy shroud). All labor and materials spent fabricating the carryover turbine base frame and making minor shop-floor tooling adjustments must be routed to a non-qualifying production cost center (Cost Center 900-PROD), preventing them from entering the denominator of the 80% fraction for HT-100B-Sub1 and HT-100B-Sub2.
Step 2: Technical Documentation Transforming Regulatory Compliance into Scientific Experimentation

In Trinity II, the second Penn Tug failed because Trinity merely showed that it switched the pilot house from aluminum to steel to comply with Coast Guard fire regulations and made downstream structural adjustments, without proving that those adjustments required systematic trial-and-error experimentation. To overcome this exact objection on HT-100B, AeroTherm must document how the regulatory material mandate created a fundamental engineering design conflict. AeroTherm's metallurgical and mechanical engineers must author a formal Pre-Design Engineering Uncertainty Memorandum demonstrating that substituting nickel-superalloy for titanium to satisfy FAA fire-penetration standards increases thermal retention by 35% and mass by 420 kilograms, which exceeds the critical whirl-speed threshold of existing rotor-bearing geometries.

Rather than relying, as Trinity did, on the bare assertion that it "experimented" with the new material without showing that the redesign involved systematic trial and error, AeroTherm must document a multi-alternative experimental protocol for HT-100B-Sub1 and HT-100B-Sub2. Specifically, the engineering team must document the concurrent design, simulation, and testing of Alternative 1 (a honeycomb-cored Inconel 718 shroud with effusion micro-cooling perforations), Alternative 2 (a dual-wall Haynes 282 shroud with a ceramic matrix composite thermal barrier coating), and Alternative 3 (an active squeeze-film damper bearing cartridge with variable-viscosity synthetic lubricant routing). AeroTherm must preserve timestamped thermal-imaging telemetry, acoustic frequency spectrograms, metallurgical grain-boundary analyses, and high-speed vibration logs from physical test-cell runs on each alternative, demonstrating a classic scientific cycle of hypothesis, physical trial, data analysis, hypothesis refinement, and retesting.
Step 3: Contract Terms and Third-Party Testing Governance

In Little Sandy Coal, amounts the taxpayer paid an outside laboratory to test welds were excluded from the credit because they were neither research nor experimental expenditures, and in Trinity Industries the court excluded the third-party-designed Intercon coupler from its evaluation and focused solely on Trinity's own research activities on the tugs. To capture 65% of outside testing and metallurgical simulation fees under I.R.C. § 41(b)(3), AeroTherm must overhaul its vendor contracts by executing Master Research Services Agreements prior to the performance of any outside destructive flame-testing or metallurgical simulation in accordance with Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2). These agreements must explicitly state that the services are being performed on behalf of AeroTherm to evaluate experimental design alternatives under AeroTherm's test protocols, rather than routine commercial code-certification or quality-control weld inspection excluded under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(D). Furthermore, the subcontractor agreements must specify that AeroTherm bears the sole financial risk of failed test iterations—paying the laboratory on a time-and-materials basis regardless of whether the shroud passes flame-impingement trials—and retains exclusive ownership of all test data, CAD models, and metallurgical process intellectual property.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Pre-Litigation Evidentiary Governance

To substantiate the claim quantitatively, AeroTherm must track all W-2 engineering wages under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and prototype superalloy raw materials consumed in destructive test-cell trials under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) directly to Component HT-100B-Sub1 and Component HT-100B-Sub2. By isolating only the two experimental subsystems via the shrinking-back rule, AeroTherm proves that 94% of the labor costs incurred on those two subcomponents constituted elements of a process of experimentation, easily surpassing the 80% threshold.

Finally, following the Fifth Circuit's definitive ruling in Trinity II that an IRS Revenue Agent Report is neither binding on the government nor entitled to a presumption of correctness in a de novo refund proceeding, AeroTherm's tax litigation counsel must treat the IRS engineer's favorable draft report as purely supplemental corroboration. AeroTherm must prepare a complete, self-contained Rule 26 Expert and Fact Witness Substantiation Package—comprising contemporaneous ERP subcomponent cost ledgers, CAD revision histories, test-cell telemetry, and sworn declarations from the lead turbine engineers—capable of proving every element of the Four-Part Test and the 80% fraction independently by a preponderance of the evidence.

cells: Whole-vessel "all-or-nothing" cost pooling; inability to quantify subcomponent costs when whole vessels failed the 80% test.
Multi-tier Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) isolating Tier 2 subsystems and Tier 3 experimental activities in a cloud-replicated ERP ledger.
Aggregating sequential Penn Tugs or assuming Coast Guard fire-code material switch (aluminum to steel) qualified the entire second tug.
Segregating sequential units into distinct components; shrinking back on Unit 2 strictly to the redesigned subsystem and documenting the engineering conflict via multi-alternative trials.
Including third-party Intercon coupler context or claiming build-to-print vessels (Hurley Dredge, LSV) without isolating internal integration R&D.
Excluding third-party vendor hardware from QREs while creating dedicated WBS shrink-back codes for internal structural/dynamic integration modeling; utilizing performance-spec contracts.

Reporting only fixed base percentages, without the underlying base period QREs or gross receipts, on amended returns; leaving non-qualified vessels in the base period; relying on an IRS RAR to carry the burden of proof.
Re-baselining historical base-period projects using the exact credit-year shrink-back filter; building a de novo trial record independent of IRS agent concessions.

body.text: Synthesis and Strategic Takeaways for U.S. Tax Practitioners

The litigation trajectory of Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States—spanning the Northern District of Texas's two-phase trial in Trinity I and the Fifth Circuit's appellate review in Trinity II—delivers an enduring dual lesson for United States corporate taxpayers and R&D tax credit advisors. On the substantive side of the ledger, Trinity Industries confirms that large-scale, custom-manufactured capital assets and first-in-class commercial vessels are not categorically barred from qualifying as experimental prototypes or pilot models under I.R.C. §§ 41 and 174, and it establishes powerful appellate precedent enforcing the two-way symmetry of the I.R.C. § 41(c)(6)(A) base-period consistency rule in the taxpayer's favor when the government or a court narrows the scope of allowable claim-year QREs.

On the evidentiary and procedural side of the ledger, however, Trinity Industries demonstrates that claiming whole-product QREs without a granular, subcomponent cost-accounting safety net is an untenable litigation gamble. Because the "substantially all" rule of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) operates as an unforgiving 80% cliff, any dilution from standard manufacturing labor, third-party hardware integration, or routine engineering modifications will disqualify the macro business component in its entirety. Unless the taxpayer has proactively structured its chart of accounts, time-tracking systems, and engineering documentation around the subcomponent hierarchy required by the shrinking-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), federal courts will decline to estimate subcomponent expenses and will sustain a 100% disallowance of the project.
